title: The Turn of the Century
tagline: Kerosene lamps, horse-drawn wagons and a one-dollar camera.

locale.persona: a farm family in the rural Midwest

morningRoutine.detail: Farmhouses had no electricity: as late as 1920 only about 2 in 100 farm homes had electric service, so light came from kerosene lamps and candles.

source.label: U.S. Census Bureau, Historical Statistics of the United States, Colonial Times to 1970, series S 108–119: dwellings with electric service

morningRoutine.detail: Children of all ages often shared one room and one teacher, walking there along country roads.

source.label: NCES, 120 Years of American Education: A Statistical Portrait (1993), Table 20

places.title: The front page
places.description: Front pages were dense columns of small type under stacked headlines. The biggest American stories of 1900 included a hurricane that killed thousands in Galveston, Texas, and a presidential election.
places.imageAlt: A dense turn-of-the-century front page with narrow columns and stacked headlines

source.label: Wikipedia: 1900 in the United States

places.title: The home
places.description: About 1.36 million telephones were in service in the United States in 1900, 17.6 per 1,000 people.
places.imageAlt: A farmhouse bedroom with a quilt-covered bed, a kerosene lamp and a washstand with a pitcher

source.label: U.S. Census Bureau, Historical Statistics of the United States, Colonial Times to 1970, series R 1-12: telephones

places.title: The street
places.description: 8,000 motor vehicles were registered in the United States in 1900.
places.imageAlt: A small-town street with a horse and buggy, a hitching rail and wooden storefronts

source.label: FHWA Highway Statistics Summary to 1995, Table MV-200: State Motor Vehicle Registrations, 1900–1995

technology.name: Brownie box camera
technology.description: Launched in February 1900 for $1, it put photography into the hands of ordinary families and children.

source.label: Science Museum Group collection: No. 1 Brownie box camera

technology.name: Telephone
technology.description: About 1.4 million telephones in 1900, fewer than 2 for every 100 people, so most farm families had none. Calls went through a switchboard operator.

source.label: U.S. Census Bureau, Historical Statistics of the United States, Colonial Times to 1970, series R 1–12: telephones

technology.name: Phonograph and gramophone
technology.description: Wind-up machines played wax cylinders or flat discs through a large horn; records had been on sale since the 1890s.

source.label: Wikipedia: Phonograph record

technology.name: Safety bicycle
technology.description: The safety bicycle, with two equal wheels and a chain drive, set off the bicycle boom of the 1890s.

source.label: Wikipedia: Safety bicycle

technology.name: Mail-order catalogue
technology.description: Thick catalogues from two Chicago mail-order houses offered farm families city goods, from cook stoves to ready-made clothing. Free rural mail delivery, begun in 1896, was still spreading.

source.label: The Henry Ford: Rural America Shops by Mail

technology.name: Typewriter
technology.description: Sold since 1874; newer machines such as the 1896 Underwood let typists see their words as they typed.

source.label: Wikipedia: Typewriter

futureVisions.prediction: Photographs will be telegraphed from any distance.
futureVisions.whoSaidIt: John Elfreth Watkins Jr., Ladies' Home Journal, December 1900
futureVisions.note: Western Union wired its first photograph in 1921 and a news wirephoto network began in 1935; today photos travel instantly.

source.label: Transcription of John Elfreth Watkins Jr., "What May Happen in the Next Hundred Years", Ladies' Home Journal, December 1900 (Playing in the World Game)

futureVisions.prediction: Americans will be taller by from one to two inches.
futureVisions.whoSaidIt: John Elfreth Watkins Jr., Ladies' Home Journal, December 1900
futureVisions.note: Even more than predicted: men born around 1900 averaged about 170 cm, men born in the 1950s–1980s about 177–179 cm, roughly 3 inches taller.

source.label: Transcription of John Elfreth Watkins Jr., "What May Happen in the Next Hundred Years", Ladies' Home Journal, December 1900 (Playing in the World Game)

futureVisions.prediction: Ready-cooked meals will be bought from establishments similar to our bakeries of today.
futureVisions.whoSaidIt: John Elfreth Watkins Jr., Ladies' Home Journal, December 1900
futureVisions.note: Restaurants, takeout and delivery now take more than half of U.S. food spending.

source.label: Transcription of John Elfreth Watkins Jr., "What May Happen in the Next Hundred Years", Ladies' Home Journal, December 1900 (Playing in the World Game)

futureVisions.prediction: There will be no C, X or Q in our everyday alphabet.
futureVisions.whoSaidIt: John Elfreth Watkins Jr., Ladies' Home Journal, December 1900
futureVisions.note: English still uses all 26 letters, C, X and Q included.

source.label: Transcription of John Elfreth Watkins Jr., "What May Happen in the Next Hundred Years", Ladies' Home Journal, December 1900 (Playing in the World Game)

futureVisions.prediction: Strawberries as large as apples will be eaten by our great-great-grandchildren.
futureVisions.whoSaidIt: John Elfreth Watkins Jr., Ladies' Home Journal, December 1900
futureVisions.note: Strawberries got bigger, but nowhere near the size of apples.

source.label: Watkins, 'What May Happen in the Next Hundred Years', Ladies' Home Journal, December 1900: transcription
